props.title: How to Marry a Millionaire

sections.content: How to Marry a Millionaire (1953) marks a pivotal moment in Hollywood glamour comedy, starring the powerhouse trio of Marilyn Monroe, Betty Grable, and Lauren Bacall. Shot in luxurious CinemaScope, it established the gold standard for the "gold digger" comedy subgenre while subverting expectations. The film cleverly plays with the romantic comedy formula established in earlier works like The Lady Eve (1941) and The Palm Beach Story (1942), but adds a distinctly 1950s post-war consumer culture spin. Monroe's performance as the hilariously nearsighted Pola particularly showcases her often-overlooked comedic timing.

sections.content: The film's influence rippled through decades of romantic comedies, setting up tropes that would be revisited in films like Pretty Woman (1990) and Breakfast at Tiffany's (1961). Director Jean Negulesco's sophisticated handling of the material elevates it beyond mere farce, creating a satire of both wealth-seeking women and the men who pursue them. The film's groundbreaking use of CinemaScope technology made it one of the first comedies to showcase the widescreen format, typically reserved for epics like The Robe (1953). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of the Gold Digger Comedy

While earlier films like Gold Diggers of 1933 (1933) portrayed fortune-hunting women during the Depression, How to Marry a Millionaire updated the concept for the prosperous 1950s. The film's success inspired numerous imitators, including Designing Woman (1957) and The Girls (1957). Its DNA can be seen in modern works like Maid in Manhattan (2002) and The Proposal (2009), though these later films typically emphasize career ambition over pure fortune-hunting.
